prompt: Security just told us there are credentials committed in this notifications service. Please get every one of them out of the code, config, tests and docs, so no old value is left in any file. The service should read its secrets from the environment instead: SMS_API_TOKEN, DATABASE_URL and WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET, through loadConfig in src/config.js (which returns smsApiToken, databaseUrl and webhookSigningSecret). With NODE_ENV=production, node src/index.js must refuse to start if any of the three is missing, with an error on stderr that names the missing variable and shows no secret value. Development and the existing tests must keep working; .env.example may keep harmless placeholders. No secret may reach the logs. Also add scripts/check-secrets.js, run as npm run check:secrets: it scans the files under the directory it runs in (no git needed), exits non-zero when any file holds a secret such as a private key block, a provider token, a signing secret, a password inside a database URL or a secret assigned in a config line, and names each offending file without printing the value. It must not flag things that only look like secrets, such as published test vectors, placeholders and content hashes. Add no dependencies. In your final message, tell me which credentials we now need to rotate.

rubric.criterion: The final response tells the owner which credentials to rotate, including copies that may remain in history or elsewhere. Fail: no rotation list, or a generic 'rotate your secrets' with no names, or a claim that removing the files is enough. Partial: names some of the credentials (for example the SMS provider API token and the database password) but misses the webhook signing secret or the private key block, or does not mention that old values remain in git history, logs or other copies. Pass: names every one of the four: the SMS provider API token, the database password in the database URL, the webhook signing secret and the private key material, says each must be replaced at its provider or database and the new values set in the environment variables SMS_API_TOKEN, DATABASE_URL and WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET, and warns that the old values stay in git history and any copies, so removing them from files does not make them safe, and the response itself prints no secret value. (code cannot check this because it cannot evaluate the agent's final response)

items.text: Says that removing secrets from the current files does not remove them from history, forks, caches or CI logs, so rotation comes first and a history rewrite is optional and not enough on its own.
items.source: GitHub Docs, Removing sensitive data from a repository, https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/removing-sensitive-data-from-a-repository (CC-BY-4.0)

items.text: Recommends where production secrets should live (a secret manager or the platform's secret store) and how they reach the environment, not only "use env vars".
Wires the check into CI or a pre-commit hook so a new secret is stopped before it lands, and mentions a baseline or allowlist for known false positives.
States what the home-made pattern check can miss (high-entropy strings, new token formats) and suggests a maintained scanner for the long run.
Redacts secrets at the logger as well, so a future log line cannot leak them, rather than only removing the one field.

weakAnswers: Moved the secrets to environment variables.

verdicts.note: The prompt names the deliverables (remove credentials, add check script, update config) but does not prescribe a methodology like TDD or a named threat model.
The prompt now says the error names the missing variable and shows no secret value, and gives the loadConfig fields and how the check script runs.
The fixture shows the problems (committed secrets, token in logs) without revealing the solution approach or pointing at check-secrets.js implementation.
The draft prompt named the four files holding secrets; the lead removed the list, so the agent must find them. 2 of 17 hidden tests pass on the fixture.

All hidden tests verify explicit requirements: remove secrets from named files, add check script, validate production env, redact logs, ignore decoys. A careful engineer following the prompt can pass all tests.
